Travel · Issue 14

The Lighthouse Coast

Nine lights, two hundred miles of granite, and the keepers’ cottages that still leave a lamp in the window.

IH
Ines Halloran10 November 2026 · 14 min read

The first light you meet on the north shore is not the brightest or the oldest, but it is the one everyone remembers. Tarrant’s Light stands at the end of Carrow Head like a chess piece someone forgot to put away: white tower, red bands, a lantern room no wider than a kitchen. When we left Port Avelin on a grey Tuesday in October, it was the last thing we saw over the stern, and it was blinking its slow, patient character — one long flash every fifteen seconds — long after the town itself had dissolved into the drizzle.

The plan was simple, which is how all bad plans begin. We would sail the length of the coast from Carrow Head to Morrow Point, a little over two hundred miles, and stop at every lighthouse along the way. Nine lights. Three weeks. One small boat, a twenty-eight-foot sloop called Whimbrel with an engine that preferred not to be discussed. We would sleep at anchor where we could and in harbors where we had to, and we would ask everyone we met the same question: what does a light mean to you now that nobody has to keep it?

The keepers who stayed

The answer, it turns out, depends on who you ask and how long they have lived within sight of one. At Kell Bay, two days north, we tied up beside a fishing boat whose skipper had grown up in the keepers’ cottage on Gannet Rock. His father kept the light for twenty-two years; his mother kept the logbook, the garden and four children, roughly in that order.

“People think it was lonely,” he told us, coiling a line with the unhurried precision of someone who has done it a hundred thousand times. “It was the opposite. Every boat that passed knew who we were. The supply launch came on Thursdays. In winter, the light was the only thing anyone on this coast could see for twelve hours a night, and we were the ones who made sure it was there.”

“In winter, the light was the only thing anyone on this coast could see for twelve hours a night.”

A keeper’s son, Kell Bay

Gannet Rock was automated in 1989. The family moved ashore, and the cottage stood empty for a decade before a local trust took it over. Today you can rent it by the week, and the guest book is a small anthology of people discovering that silence has a texture. One entry, from a February a few years ago, simply reads: Wind all night. Light all night. Slept like a child.

Reading the coast by night

Every lighthouse has a character: a pattern of flashes, eclipses and colors that tells a navigator exactly which light they are looking at. Tarrant’s is a single long flash. Gannet Rock shows two short white flashes every ten seconds. Skerry Holm, out on its own at the edge of the sound, is a group of three. Learn them and the dark coast becomes a sentence you can read.

We learned them the way everyone does, by getting them wrong. On our fourth night, beating into a short sea off Morrow Sands, I counted three flashes, checked the almanac, and confidently announced that we were six miles further north than we were. My partner, who had been quietly timing the eclipses with the stopwatch on her phone, pointed out that the flashes were red. The light was the harbor entrance at Saltness, and the rocks I had been so sure we were clear of were a mile off the bow. We tacked. Nobody spoke for a while.

It is easy to forget how much information a single light carries. Its color tells you the sector you are in; its rhythm tells you its name; its height, read against the chart, tells you roughly how far away it is when it first lifts over the horizon. A good navigator a century ago could fix a position from two lights and a watch, and many still do it for the pleasure of the thing.

Granite, gulls and good bread

By the second week we had found the rhythm of the coast. Mornings were for sailing, while the land breeze held. Afternoons were for walking up to whichever light we had reached, usually by a path that started politely and ended in heather up to the knees. Evenings were for finding bread, which on the north shore is a serious undertaking: the villages are small, the bakeries are smaller, and most of them sell out by ten.

The exception is the bakery at Holm Quay, which opens at five in the morning for the ferry crews and keeps baking until the flour runs out. We bought a seeded loaf the size of a fender and ate half of it walking back to the boat. The baker, who also runs the post office and the island’s only taxi, recommended the walk to the light at the north end of the island. “Go at sunset,” she said. “Take a jumper. Don’t feed the gulls.”

We did as we were told, mostly. The light at Holm North is the smallest on the coast — a squat white tower barely taller than a house — but it stands on a shelf of pink granite above the whole outer sound, and at sunset the islands to the west go from gold to violet to black while you watch. A pair of gannets worked the tide race below us. A seal surfaced, considered us, and left.

Know before you go

  • When: May to September for settled weather; October for empty anchorages and early dark.
  • Charts: The 1:50,000 Sound of Avelin sheet covers Carrow Head to Kell Bay. Carry the larger-scale harbor plans for Saltness and Holm Quay.
  • Staying ashore: The cottages at Gannet Rock and Tarrant’s Light are let by the harbor trust. Book early for summer.
  • Tides: Streams in the inshore passage reach three knots at springs. Plan the narrows at slack water.

The last light

Morrow Point is where the coast gives up and turns east, and its lighthouse is the tallest of the nine: one hundred and twelve steps to the gallery, each of them a little narrower than the last. A volunteer from the trust unlocked the door for us and waited at the bottom, which we took as a comment on our fitness.

From the top you can see the whole of the north shore laid out behind you, every headland and bay we had spent three weeks working past, compressed into a single blue line. Somewhere back there, past the curve of the earth, Tarrant’s Light was flashing its long, slow flash to nobody in particular.

That, I think, is the answer to the question we had been asking. A lighthouse no longer needs a keeper, and most ships no longer need a lighthouse. But the lights are still there, every night, doing exactly what they promised to do. On a coast where the weather changes four times before lunch, there is something steadying about that. You look up, you count the flashes, and you know where you are. ■
